b: It’s telling that Jared Bush, chief creative officer of Walt Disney Animation Studios, co-wrote Hexed, because, narratively speaking, the studio’s latest feature feels cobbled together from commercially guaranteed, off-the-shelf parts. It’s yet another chronicle of a Disney princess, though Billie Doe (voiced by Hailee Steinfeld) has the kind of spunky edge, shot through with vulnerability, that marked such pop-culture heroines as Buffy the Vampire Slayer. And female empowerment is once again a major theme, with Billie, like Frozen’s Elsa, discovering her own strength as a witch while contending with both her overprotective mother, Alice (Rashida Jones), and Celeste (Jodie Foster), the power-hungry queen of a magical realm.

As its title suggests, Hexed revolves around witches, and much of the film takes place in Hexe, an alternate universe meant as a utopia where witches and wizards can live their identities. It’s currently under the authoritarian rule of Queen Celeste, who claims to be the only witch who can fly, and thus the only one who can spread that ability to the masses, as Hexe’s founder intended. Billie’s sudden arrival in Hexe, however, punctures that claim when she’s caught flying in public, which is enough to convince the realm’s residents that she’s the real “chosen one,” who, once aligned with a full moon, can fulfill its founder’s dream of universal flight.

Billie has been sucked into Hexe from suburban Ohio, where she and Alice have lived in uneasy normalcy since her mother moved them out of their original home in (where else?) Salem, Massachusetts, when Billie was a toddler. Billie has grown into a rebellious teenager who chafes against her mother’s restrictions. But when she gets wind of her powers—kept in check by a wristband with a purple pearl that accidentally comes off one day at school—her journey through Hexe leads her to the truth about her lineage. Not only is Alice, who follows her daughter into the realm to retrieve her, also a witch, but Billie is Queen Celeste’s granddaughter, Alice having fled her mother’s emotionally abusive clutches after becoming pregnant.

There are hints in Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller’s script of the kind of social allegory that distinguished the Zootopia movies. Queen Celeste could be seen as a Trump avatar, her ruthless drive to maintain control of Hexe tied to her need to keep up the appearance of having special powers, even though she basically stole them from her daughter. She even has a sycophantic, big-gutted buffoon of a second-in-command, Hieronymous (Dan Stevens). Her craving for absolute rule also enforces a rough class structure: Those who live farther from the castle have weaker powers than those who live closer, while animals have been banished to a neighborhood of their own. None of these gestures are imagined with the thoroughness that made the first Zootopia stand out, but the absence of heavy-handedness could count as a blessing.

Unfortunately, a similar lack of rigor extends to the film’s characterizations and world-building. Flashbacks show Celeste browbeating Alice as a child to the point that she easily convinced her daughter to transfer her powers to her, but why that led Alice to flee Hexe after becoming pregnant with Billie is left hazy at best. Even hazier is Celeste’s own backstory, relegated to one offhand mention of neglectful parents, which evokes that moth-eaten justification of “family trauma.” And then there’s the nature of witches’ powers in this film: There appear to be no limits on what they can do, which leeches away any sense of genuine danger.

The film’s images and sounds offer only partial compensation for these dramatic shortcomings. In keeping with that purple-pearl wristband, a purplish tint dominates much of the imagery under Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand’s direction, suggesting a queer angle to Billie’s coming-of-age quest that never adds up to much but is nevertheless pleasing to the eye. The animation has its pleasures, but even the most gorgeous visuals—including a sequence in which Billie and Alice fly together that should have been the film’s transcendent emotional high point—aren’t given room to breathe amid the frantic pacing. And when a climactic sequence is scored to Queen’s uptempo “I Want to Break Free,” robbing the moment of the dramatic weight it deserved, Hexed exposes itself as the formulaic corporate product it is at heart.

Cast: Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones, Jodie Foster, Walton Goggins, Henry Winkler, Dan Stevens, Brett Gelman, Tracey Ullman, Stephen Fry Director: Fawn Veerasunthorn, Jason Hand Screenwriter: Jared Bush, Dana Ledoux Miller Distributor: Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures Running Time: 103 min Rating: PG Year: 2026
